content: Amnesic shellfish poisoning (ASP) is one of the four recognized syndromes of shellfish poisoning, primarily associated with bivalve mollusks such as mussels, clams, oysters, and scallops. These shellfish are filter feeders, meaning they accumulate toxins produced by microscopic algae, including dinoflagellates and diatoms. ASP occurs as a result of consuming domoic acid, a neurotoxin. In the brain, domoic acid particularly damages the hippocampus and amygdaloid nucleus by activating AMPA and kainate receptors, leading to an influx of calcium into neurons. While calcium influx is a normal cellular process, the uncontrolled increase caused by domoic acid results in neuronal degeneration. This toxin can bioaccumulate in marine organisms that consume phytoplankton, such as shellfish, anchovies, and sardines. In mammals, including humans, domoic acid acts as a neurotoxin, causing permanent short-term memory loss, brain damage, and, in severe cases, death. Harmful algal blooms are closely linked to the occurrence of ASP. Importantly, cooking or freezing contaminated fish or shellfish does not reduce the toxicity of domoic acid. ASP was first identified in late 1987 during a significant outbreak of food poisoning in eastern Canada. This outbreak resulted in the deaths of three elderly patients and left other victims with long-term neurological complications. Due to the memory loss associated with the condition, the term amnesic shellfish poisoning was coined to describe this clinical syndrome. The incident received widespread media attention. Epidemiologists from Health Canada quickly traced the illnesses to restaurant meals containing cultured mussels harvested from a specific area in Prince Edward Island, a region previously unaffected by toxic algae. Mouse bioassays using extracts from the suspect mussels revealed unusual neurotoxic symptoms distinct from those caused by paralytic shellfish poisoning or other known toxins. On December 12, 1987, a team of scientists convened at the National Research Council of Canada laboratory in Halifax, Nova Scotia. By December 16, just four days into their investigation, the team identified the toxin using bioassay-directed fractionation and chemical analysis. Domoic acid poisoning has also been implicated in other unusual events. For example, on June 22, 2006, a California brown pelican, possibly affected by domoic acid, collided with a car windshield on the Pacific Coast Highway. The toxin is known to be present in local marine environments. Additionally, domoic acid poisoning may have contributed to a 1961 incident in Santa Cruz, California, where thousands of frenzied seabirds invaded the area. This event reportedly inspired Alfred Hitchcock's 1963 film The Birds, based on Daphne du Maurier's novella. The clinical presentation of ASP begins with gastrointestinal symptoms, which typically appear within 24 hours of consuming mollusks contaminated with domoic acid. These symptoms include vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and, in some cases, hemorrhagic gastritis. In more severe cases, neurological symptoms develop after a delay of several hours to three days. These symptoms include headache, dizziness, disorientation, visual disturbances, short-term memory loss, motor weakness, seizures, excessive respiratory secretions, hiccups, unstable blood pressure, cardiac arrhythmias, and coma. Treatment for ASP is primarily supportive, as there is no antidote for domoic acid. Patients exposed to high doses of the toxin or those with risk factors such as advanced age or renal failure are at increased risk of death. Among 107 confirmed cases, four fatalities were reported. In some survivors, permanent sequelae include short-term memory loss and peripheral polyneuropathy. Management focuses on addressing symptoms and preventing complications.
